title: Work: The Scientific Definition
lead: Writing an exam and carrying a heavy load across level ground are hard work in the everyday sense, and neither is work in the scientific sense. This section gives the definition a scientist uses: a force does work on a system only when the system is displaced and the force has a component along that displacement, and the work is that component multiplied by the distance the force acts through. It also shows when the work is positive, when it is zero and when it is negative, and gives work and energy their unit, the joule.
objectives: Explain how an object must be displaced for a force on it to do work.
Explain how relative directions of force and displacement determine whether the work done is positive, negative, or zero.
summary_html:
• Work is the transfer of energy by a force acting on an object as it is displaced.
  • The work $\kW$ that a force $\kF$ does on an object is the product of the magnitude $\kF$ of the force, times the magnitude $\kd$ of the displacement, times the cosine of the angle $\theta$ between them. In symbols, $$\kW = \kF\kd\cos\theta.$$
  • The SI unit for work and energy is the joule (J), where $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$.
  • The work done by a force is zero if the displacement is either zero or perpendicular to the force.
  • The work done is positive if the force and displacement have the same direction, and negative if they have opposite direction.

figures.original_caption: Examples of work. (a) The work done by the force F on this lawn mower is Fd cos θ. Note that F cos θ is the component of the force in the direction of motion. (b) A person holding a briefcase does no work on it, because there is no displacement. No energy is transferred to or from the briefcase. (c) The person moving the briefcase horizontally at a constant speed does no work on it, and transfers no energy to it. (d) Work is done on the briefcase by carrying it up stairs at constant speed, because there is necessarily a component of force F in the direction of the motion. Energy is transferred to the briefcase and could in turn be used to do work. (e) When the briefcase is lowered, energy is transferred out of the briefcase and into an electric generator. Here the work done on the briefcase by the generator is negative, removing energy from the briefcase, because F and d are in opposite directions.

exercises.prompt: Before railroads were invented, goods often traveled along canals, with mules pulling barges from the bank. If a mule is exerting a 1200 N force for 10 km, and the rope connecting the mule to the barge is at a 20 degree angle from the direction of travel, how much work did the mule do on the barge?

answer.hint: The rope is not along the direction of travel, so only the component of the force along the displacement does work, and the distance is in kilometres rather than metres.

exercises.prompt: Describe an instance today in which you did work, by the scientific definition. Then calculate how much work you did in that instance, showing your work.

answer.solution: Look for a moment when you exerted a force on something and that something moved, since both are needed before any work is done at all. Lifting a backpack from the floor onto a desk is a convenient instance, because the force you exert is the weight of the pack and the displacement is straight up, so the angle between them is zero and the cosine is one. Weigh the pack, or estimate its mass; a full school pack is about 5 kg, so the force needed to lift it steadily is $\kF = mg = (5\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2) = 49\ \text{N}$. Measure the height of the desk, about 0.75 m. Then $\kW = \kF\kd\cos\theta = (49\ \text{N})(0.75\ \text{m})\cos 0^\circ = 37\ \text{J}$, which is a little more than the energy in a hundredth of a food calorie. Any instance will do, so long as you name the force, measure or estimate the distance it acted through, and state the angle between the two.

exercises.prompt: You have a cart track, a cart, several masses, and a position-sensing pulley. Design an experiment to examine how the force exerted on the cart does work as it moves through a distance.

answer.solution: Hang a known mass from a string that runs over the position-sensing pulley and is tied to the cart, so that the weight of the hanging mass is the force pulling the cart along the track. The string is parallel to the track, so the angle between the force and the displacement is zero and the work done on the cart is simply $\kW = \kF\kd$. Release the cart from rest and let the pulley record its position as it travels, and read off the distance the cart has moved at several instants. Multiplying that distance by the known force gives the work done up to each instant, and a graph of the work against the distance should be a straight line whose slope is the force. Repeat with a heavier hanging mass and the line should be steeper, since the same distance now takes more work, and repeat over a longer stretch of track and the work should grow in proportion to the distance.

exercises.prompt: You have a cart track, two carts, several masses, a position-sensing pulley, and a piece of carpet (a rough surface) that will fit over the track. Design an experiment to examine how the force exerted on the cart does work as the cart moves through a distance.

answer.solution: Run the experiment twice, once on the bare track and once with the carpet laid over it, and pull the cart each time with the same known force, the weight of a mass hanging from a string over the position-sensing pulley. The string is parallel to the track, so the work the string does on the cart is $\kW = \kF\kd$ in both runs, and for the same distance it is the same number. What changes is that the carpet exerts a force of friction on the cart in the direction opposite to the motion, so the angle between that force and the displacement is $180^\circ$, its cosine is $-1$, and the work friction does is negative: it takes energy out of the cart rather than putting energy in. The second cart lets you add mass to the one being pulled and see that a heavier cart presses harder on the carpet, so the friction force and the negative work it does both grow while the work done by the string stays the same.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of something we think of as work in everyday circumstances that is not work in the scientific sense. Is energy transferred or changed in form in your example? If so, explain how this is accomplished without doing work.

answer.solution: Holding a heavy box steady at chest height is hard work in the everyday sense, and it is no work at all in the scientific sense, because the box is not displaced: $\kd = 0$, so $\kW = 0$ however long you stand there. Energy is certainly transferred, but not to the box. The muscles that hold your arms up do not stay contracted in one piece; their fibres release and take hold again many times a second, so the muscles are doing work against one another inside your body, and the chemical energy your food supplied is going into thermal energy rather than into the box. The box gains nothing, which is why you could put it down and find it exactly as it was.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of a situation in which there is a force and a displacement, but the force does no work. Explain why it does no work.

answer.solution: Carry a briefcase at a constant speed along level ground. The force your hand exerts on the case is upward, since it is holding the case against gravity, and the displacement is horizontal, so the angle between them is $90^\circ$. Because $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, the work is $\kW = \kF\kd\cos 90^\circ = 0$: there is a force and there is a displacement, but the force has no component in the direction of the motion, so no energy is transferred to the briefcase. A satellite in a circular orbit is the same situation on a larger scale, since the gravitational force on it always points at the centre of the circle and the motion is always along the circle.

exercises.prompt: Describe a situation in which a force is exerted for a long time but does no work. Explain.

answer.solution: Push against a parked car as hard as you like for an hour. The car does not move, so the displacement is zero and the work you do on it is $\kW = \kF(0)\cos\theta = 0$, no matter how large the force is or how long you keep it up. Work is not force and it is not effort over time; it is a force acting through a distance, and without displacement in the direction of the force there is no distance for it to act through and no energy transferred to the car. The energy you spend goes into your own muscles, which warm as they work against one another.

exercises.prompt: How much work does a supermarket checkout attendant do on a can of soup he pushes 0.600 m horizontally with a force of 5.00 N? Express your answer in joules and kilocalories.

answer.hint: The push and the displacement are both horizontal, so the angle between them is zero and $\cos\theta = 1$. One food calorie is 4186 J.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the work done on a 1500-kg elevator car by its cable to lift it 40.0 m at constant speed, assuming friction averages 100 N. (b) What is the work done on the elevator car by the gravitational force in this process? (c) What is the total work done on the elevator car?

parts.part: (a) the work done by the cable
parts.hint: At constant speed the cable must balance the weight and the friction together, and it pulls in the direction the car moves.

parts.part: (b) the work done by the gravitational force
parts.hint: The gravitational force points down while the car goes up, so the angle between them is $180^\circ$.

figure.caption: A man pushes a crate up a ramp.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the work done by an 85.0-kg man who pushes a crate 4.00 m up along a ramp that makes an angle of $20.0^\circ$ with the horizontal, as shown in the figure. He exerts a force of 500 N on the crate parallel to the ramp and moves at a constant speed. Be certain to include the work he does on the crate and on his body to get up the ramp.

answer.hint: The 500 N push is parallel to the ramp, so it does work over the whole 4.00 m; the man also lifts his own weight through the height the ramp gains.

exercises.prompt: A shopper pushes a grocery cart 20.0 m at constant speed on level ground, against a 35.0 N frictional force. He pushes in a direction $25.0^\circ$ below the horizontal. (a) What is the work done on the cart by friction? (b) What is the work done on the cart by the gravitational force? (c) What is the work done on the cart by the shopper? (d) Find the force the shopper exerts, using energy considerations. (e) What is the total work done on the cart?

parts.hint: Friction opposes the motion, so the angle between it and the displacement is $180^\circ$.

parts.part: (b) the work done by the gravitational force
parts.hint: The ground is level, so the weight is perpendicular to the displacement.

parts.part: (c) the work done by the shopper

parts.hint: Only the component of his push along the motion does work, so divide the work he does by $\kd\cos 25.0^\circ$.

parts.part: (e) the total work done on the cart
